title: one question, end to end
question: what is decentralized ai?
answer: ai that runs on machines nobody owns together. strangers do the work, and a shared ledger keeps score and pays them.
about: we follow one question through a decentralized network, from the gateway to the machine that answers it to the ledger that pays.

title: three ways to trust an answer
question: how do you trust an answer you did not compute?
answer: three ways: a math proof, a sealed chip, or many checkers who stake money on their verdict.
about: we compare the three ways to verify ai work that someone else ran: zero-knowledge proofs, sealed hardware and staked scoring.

title: skin in the game
question: why would strangers be honest?
answer: each one puts money down first, and lying loses it.
about: we explain stake, slashing and rewards, and why together they make honesty the cheaper choice.

title: the oracle pattern
question: how does a blind ledger learn about the world?
answer: staked reporters, and lying made more expensive than the truth.
about: we show how a blockchain gets facts from the outside world, from price feeds to ai scores.

title: why building the model is harder
question: why is building a model harder than using it?
answer: training makes machines talk to each other all the time. using a model does not.
about: we explain why training a model across the internet is much harder than running one.

title: airbnb for gpus
question: who does the work?
answer: people who rent out their own gpus. a network sends them jobs and pays per job.
about: we look at open markets for renting gpus, and what makes renting from strangers safe.

title: agents with wallets
question: can software use it on its own?
answer: yes. agents now get wallets, names and signed permission to spend.
about: we explain what an ai agent is, and what changes when it gets its own wallet and identity.

title: who decides?
question: who decides on a network with no boss?
answer: token holders vote, until the first real fight over the rules.
about: we look at how a network with no company sets its rules, and where that can break.

title: the off-switch
question: can anyone switch ai off?
answer: yes. one government order did it, for everyone outside one country.
about: a government order cut off a frontier model outside one country, in the same week a tiny open model won at one task.

title: when a network sells itself
question: what happens when a network pays in its own token?
answer: it sells a little of itself every block.
about: we explain how paying rewards in a network's own token pushes its price down, and what reinvesting the rewards changes.

title: the permission slip
question: who decides who gets the strongest models?
answer: one government review now does.
about: the us began reviewing who gets access to frontier models, and we look at what that means for open alternatives.

title: why the frontier stays in one room
question: can strangers train a frontier model together?
answer: not yet. sharing the work costs more than doing it.
about: we explain why frontier training needs one data centre, and the tricks that try to spread it across the internet.

title: the third rail
question: how does an agent pay?
answer: on two rival rails, both built on an unused corner of the web.
about: two rival groups launched ways for ai agents to pay on their own, both built on the old http 402 status code.

title: train your own
question: why own a model at all?
answer: renting is cheap to start, but the landlord sets the terms.
about: prime intellect raised 130 million dollars on the bet that companies will train their own models.

title: the scorekeeper
question: what is scarce in training an agent?
answer: a trustworthy judge of its work. not the computer.
about: we explain why the hard part of training ai agents is judging their work, not finding the compute.

title: a name and a wallet
question: what does an agent need to do business?
answer: a wallet and a name. only the name is hard to fake.
about: agent payments and agent identities both reached real scale, and we ask which of the two is hard to fake.

title: the name that stays
question: how does an agent earn a reputation?
answer: one public number that stays the same and is costly to abandon.
about: we explain how an agent keeps one reputation across many services with a single stable identifier.

title: no handshake required
question: does a server need to remember the agent?
answer: no. every request now says everything, every time.
about: the mcp specification removed sessions, so any server can answer any agent, and we look at what that changes.

title: say yes once
question: who allowed the agent to try?
answer: a signed, bounded permission that a stranger can check days later.
about: we explain how a person's permission for an agent becomes a signed, limited token that others can check.

title: the gate was never the license
question: is an open model really open?
answer: only if you have the memory to run it. pooling memory means checking strangers.
about: the largest open model ever released stayed out of reach because of memory, and a network of gaming gpus claims a way around it.

title: nobody checks the answer
question: does anyone check every answer?
answer: no. one possible check hangs over every answer, and lying stops paying.
about: we explain optimistic verification: why most answers are never checked, and why the threat of a check is enough.

title: nobody to trust
question: what does privacy cost?
answer: one lab priced it at 12.5x. a network with no "us" had to prove it instead.
about: a frontier lab offered a 12.5x discount to train on your data, and we compare it with networks that prove privacy instead.

title: the wiring between them
question: why is joining two safe systems unsafe?
answer: the paid party can now reach the instrument that measures it.
about: we explain why connecting two safe incentive systems can make both of them unsafe.

title: somebody has to sign
question: who signs a license for a network?
answer: nobody. there is no one standing there to hand it to.
about: one lab released two models under two licenses, and we explain why a license is a limit open networks cannot route around.

title: the entry fee
question: is there a check that needs no trust?
answer: a proof. but the model has to be made countable first.
about: we explain zero-knowledge proofs for ai, and the cost of turning a model into something a proof can cover.

title: the easy half
question: can useful ai work replace proof of work?
answer: only if it stays as easy to check.
about: we look at proposals to replace proof-of-work mining with useful ai work, and why checking is the hard part.

title: hardware attestation
question: what does a sealed chip prove?
answer: that the room was right, not that the answer was right.
about: we explain trusted execution environments: what sealed hardware proves, what it does not, and why customers use it first.

title: compute as collateral
question: who buys the machines?
answer: strangers on a chain, backed by a receipt.
about: gpu purchases are now funded by investors on a chain, and we look at the receipt that is meant to secure them.

title: counterfactual verification
question: did the work make any difference?
answer: the first instrument that asks runs a second party to compare.
about: a new paper proposes checking whether ai work changed the outcome at all, not only whether it was done.

title: stake delegation
question: who votes with staked tokens?
answer: often whoever holds them for you, not you.
about: money flowed into a network through staking products, and we follow who ended up holding the votes.

title: the stake-weighted middle
question: how do strangers agree on one score?
answer: cut the extremes and keep the stake-weighted middle.
about: we explain how a network turns many validators' scores into one number by trimming to the stake-weighted median.

title: attestation vs re-execution
question: which way of checking is winning?
answer: neither removes trust. each one picks what to trust.
about: re-running work got easier and hardware attestation got forged in the same weeks, and we compare the two.

title: memory access patterns
question: can a sealed chip still leak?
answer: yes. the order it touches memory can spell out your prompt.
about: we explain side channels: how watching memory access inside a sealed machine can reveal your prompt.

title: the inference subsidy
question: why is open ai so cheap to use?
answer: the network prints its own token and sells it.
about: we look at how open inference is sold below cost, and a proposal to pay for it with credits that only work inside the network.

title: could not check
question: what should a checker say when it cannot check?
answer: a third answer. with only yes or no, it lies.
about: we explain why a checker needs a third answer, "could not check", beside yes and no.

title: canonical serialization
question: why do honest parties look like liars?
answer: a fingerprint covers bytes, not meaning.
about: we explain why two honest parties can produce different fingerprints of the same work, and how a canonical format fixes it.

title: integer overflow
question: can a guard made from the same arithmetic catch the theft?
answer: no. it overflowed in step with the money.
about: an automated auditor found a flaw that minted 184 times a network's supply, and we look at why the guard missed it.

title: nothing left to compare
question: what is lost when a network stops comparing its judges?
answer: the one thing that made a bad judgment cost anything.
about: we explain how a network turns many judgments into one payment, and what an owner's new switch removes.

title: the pay split
question: who pays when a network lets every project set its own cut?
answer: the people behind the judges. one share is fixed first.
about: bittensor lets each sub-network set its own pay split, and we explain why one share is held in place and who absorbs the change.
